summary:
The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to the territory, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, carrying maximum terms of seven years and five years respectively, with consent explicitly not a defence. Coverage of the later repeal described the exposure under the 1969 Act as up to ten years. The penalty figures reported for the 1969 provisions differ across the sources; all agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands. The same bill also added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Marriage between same-sex partners remains barred under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000. A visitor travelling with a same-sex spouse should expect no recognition of that relationship under Cook Islands law.

The sources record no criminal penalty attaching to consensual adult same-sex conduct after 1 June 2023, and no evidence of any prosecution under sections 154 or 155.
tangentialFactors:
Repeal followed a reform effort that ran for at least six years and reversed course repeatedly. A draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand assistance, would have removed sections 154 and 155; a 2017 select committee recommended striking them, along with the provisions on indecent acts between men and sodomy, from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the report was deferred again in October 2020, when MPs pushed the Crimes Bill report out by three months.

Parliament opened public submissions on the Crimes Bill in August 2017 as part of an effort to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed that a submission from the Te Tiare Association, representing the territory's LGBTI community, was already before the select committee, and at least three lawyers were expected to address penalties and sentencing.

Reporting on the colonial history of the offence states that colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society. The territory's population is around 21,000.
localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association, described as the territory's only LGBTI community group, welcomed the 2017 draft decriminalisation bill. Its member Valentino Wichman was quoted on the homophobic character of the Crimes Act provisions.

The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 bars same-sex marriage for residents as well as visitors, so the repeal of sections 154 and 155 did not open a marital recognition route for same-sex couples locally.

The Crimes Amendment Bill that removed the male-conduct offences also strengthened protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault, and those provisions apply to residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific legal provision appears anywhere in the sourced material. Whether the Cook Islands have rules on legal gender recognition, identity documents and marker changes, bathroom and facility access, restrictions or bans on gender-affirming health care, hate-crime or hate-speech coverage of gender identity, or entry and immigration screening that could expose a trans visitor's status is unresolved and not sourced.

The maximum penalty recorded for sections 154 and 155 of the 1969 Crimes Act differs between sources, seven and five years in the earlier reporting against ten years in the 2023 reporting. This discrepancy is unresolved within the inventory.

The extent to which New Zealand-origin statutes extend to the Cook Islands, particularly any anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, is not sourced.
